records.l: Toto, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Toto is a very good, fresh and cheery young boy, a child of the family and the blind grandmother's boy and companion. He helps his grandmother with longstanding household work, is proud of her, and loves the forest deeply. With curly hair, honest gray eyes, ruddy-brown cheeks, marbles in his pockets, a whistle, and an old fiddle inherited from his grandfather, he is a merry whistler and capable fiddler. He also inherited a porringer from his great-grandfather, owns the Black Spanish chickens, and has known the cow-and-moon rhyme since infancy. In winter, Toto comes home with Bruin carrying milk, after splitting kindling, building a snow fort, and snowballing with him; he helps make supper and listens to Granny's story. He is imaginative and eager for stories, wishing he had been Chop-Chin, requesting a fairy story from the hermit, and later telling The Naughty Comet after identifying a comet but admitting he does not know exactly what comets are. His friendship with Bruin began in childhood after Toto fought a wild-cat at seven and then met Bruin and the raccoon. He is hospitable to the raccoon, offering his bed as a foot-warmer, lending him a red cravat, and later reassuring Mr. Woodmouse, Senior, that the raccoon means no harm. Toto joins Cracker and the raccoon at the woodmouse family wedding, where he provides lively fiddle music, dances with the raccoon, and receives checkerberries, nuts, and messages of regret and apology to Bruin. He conducts a dancing-school lesson, plays and demonstrates the steps, and joins other festivities. He also proves helpful and brave: traveling with Bruin to Baldhead's cave, entering first, bringing water and jelly, and feeding Baldhead until he recovers. He returns home with Jim Crow, praises <DW53>, Miss Mary, and Cracker, and later visits the hermit with the crow and food for Bruin. He recognizes Ger-Falcon as the hawk that tried to take his chickens. At the cottage party he gathers eggs, decorates, plays for the birds' quadrille, and games with the others. Though saddened that spring may separate him from forest life and distressed when Bruin seems to leave without farewell, he finds Bruin in the wood-shed. Bruin stays, and Toto continues visiting the forest and sharing its happenings with his grandmother.

records.l: Bruin, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Bruin is a huge, shaggy black bear with a kind heart, great strength, and a clumsy build. He is Toto’s longtime friend and the blind grandmother’s faithful helper and protector, living permanently in their little cottage. Although large enough to seem frightening, he has lost his taste for killing and repeatedly acts with care: he cooks supper, tends the fire and cottage, protects others, carries food to the injured Baldhead, cares for the hermit, rescues the raccoon, and spares Ger-Falcon after learning the hawk was starving. At the cottage, Bruin takes on extensive household work, including washing, churning, baking, brewing, milking, tending the pig, and preparing meals. He sleeps on the hearth-rug, does not hibernate because the Madam would disapprove, and enjoys company, stories, games, and Russian backgammon. His size causes comic difficulties: dancing school leaves him sore, he cannot master the waltz, and he ruins the grandmother’s custard pie when he falls on it. Yet he remains willing to practice and help, serving as a step-ladder, polishing the floor with brushes on his feet, and wearing a red rose in his left ear. By the end, when the animals depart, Bruin cannot say goodbye. He hides in the wood-shed and splits excessive kindling, explaining that he cannot leave Toto, the blind grandmother, the calf, the pig, or the cottage work. He stays with the grandmother and settles permanently as her devoted friend, protector, and domestic helper.

records.l: <DW53>, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: <DW53> is a handsome, dark-furred raccoon and Toto’s enduring animal companion, household helper, and friend. Bright-eyed and usually good-hearted despite a love of jokes, he wears a red cravat or scarlet neck-ribbon and later a scarlet feather given by Miss Mary. He fears Toto’s tea-kettle as if it were alive after burning his paw on it, yet performs cottage chores: sweeping the hearth or using his tail for sweeping, setting the table, catching rats, and polishing the kettle. Saving and unable to bear waste, he is deeply upset when his saved squash pie disappears; after learning that brown mice ate it, he plans to send them from the cellar to the forest. He refuses to sweep red-hot coals, choosing to tell the story of the Useful Coal instead, then joins dancing lessons. With Toto and Cracker, he attends the woodmouse wedding in Toto’s cravat, enjoys the attention, treats the couple graciously, and waltzes with Toto. He questions and sarcastically challenges Toto’s explanation of a comet, listens to stories, and is praised for helping defend the cottage during an attempted robbery. Near the end, he helps decorate the cottage, recounts falling through a hollow tree while gathering honey, and joins the games. He also enjoys chasing cats and curls his beautiful tail about his toes or over his back.

records.l: Granny, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Granny is Toto’s blind, old and beloved grandmother, a family member who lives with Toto and the animals in a little cottage. She has snowy curls, an armchair in the warm chimney-corner, and, on special occasions, wears gold-bowed spectacles and uses an ebony stick. Her evenings center on knitting by the blazing hearth, working at a spinning-wheel, and telling the grandmother’s story, which she herself learned from her grandmother. At first she comes from her room with a squirrel on her shoulder, joins supper, and begins a story while enjoying the easier life the animals’ help has given her. She guides the household: she explains a Chinese pig-tail, sends everyone to bed, has Bruin cover the fire and lock the house, worries over disturbances and possible injuries, and later helps settle Toto and Cracker’s dispute. She welcomes Toto home, joins the group around the fire, and helps complete a poem. For a supper with guests, she prepares pastries, oversees the meal, and dresses carefully. By the end, she thanks the animals for their winter comfort and help, mourns Bruin’s apparent departure, then joyfully welcomes him back to live with her and Toto.

records.l: Cracker, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Cracker is a little squirrel, also described as a boy, who lives in a cottage with Toto and Bruin. He has sharp teeth, access to nuts in the barn-chamber, enjoys waltzing, attends Toto’s grandmother when idle, and tells household stories. After angrily denying that he took squash pie and threatening to bite ears and throw cheese, he is rebuked and ashamed. At dancing school he learns jumps and foot changes, then whirls Miss Mary while waltzing until they stumble against Bruin’s paw. At a wedding he greets woodland guests, defends Mrs. Cow and Toto’s food, and dances with a young red squirrel. He wonders about a comet, urges help for Baldhead after hearing of his broken leg and hunger, helps after a robbery, and recounts Mrs. Cow’s moon story despite Toto’s interruption.

records.l: Pigeon Pretty, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Pigeon Pretty, a gentle wood-pigeon, perches in Toto's cottage, is chased by a large hawk, collapses at Bruin's feet, asks mercy for starving Ger-Falcon, and recovers on the hermit's knee.

records.l: Miss Mary, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Miss Mary is a parrot living in Central Africa and perched at a comfortable window perch in Toto's cottage. The family considers her sober-minded, though she is not specially affectionate; she is fond of Pigeon Pretty and is married to Miss Mary's husband. Her father, Polacko, is reputed to have a notable beak and, she says, escaped China after a mandarin's grandson tried to make him eat with chopsticks. After two tail feathers are bitten off while she sleeps, Miss Mary silently lets two brown mice eat the squash pie. She disdains dancing until Cracker seizes and whirls her, whereupon she threatens to peck his eyes out and returns to her perch. She then confronts a robber, helps defend the cottage, and thanks Bruin after he saves her life, changing from bad terms to friendship. Finally, she tells The Three Remarks.

records.l: Chucky, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Chucky, a hungry, peevish woodchuck, customarily hibernates in winter in Toto's cupboard, where he is trapped in worsted, freed by the wood-pigeon, eats, samples dishes, and joins games.

records.l: the cottage, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The cottage contains a cellar, cupboard, kitchen, and grandmother's room. It is home to inhabitants troubled by mice in the cupboard and cellar, and it becomes quiet at night as mice enter the kitchen and its windows rattle. A robber later disorders the kitchen while searching it, but the occupants restore it. Finally, the cottage is decorated and prepared as the setting for a party with supper, games, stories, and dancing.

records.l: kitchen (Toto's cottage), Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The kitchen is Toto's cottage's warm, bright household center, with a great hearth fire, kettle, cookware, food stores, and silverware. In winter the family and animals gather there for supper and stories; later a robber searches it, but Miss Mary, the raccoon, and the kettle drive him out.

records.l: the cupboard, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The cupboard holds a saved piece of squash pie until brown mice enter through a door crack and gnaw it.

records.l: fire (Toto's cottage hearth), Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A great, bright hearth fire crackles and leaps, lighting the kitchen and making its objects glitter as Bruin tends it and the group gathers in comfort. Before sleep, Bruin carefully covers it with ashes; its embers retain a dusky glow as mice seek warmth.

records.l: soup-kettle (Toto's cottage), Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A black soup-kettle hangs over Toto's cottage hearth, bubbling as Bruin stirs its savory onion stew; its ordinary business is making soup from good ingredients.

records.l: tea-kettle (Toto's cottage), Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A remarkable, brightly burnished copper tea-kettle sits on Toto's cottage hearth, polished by Bruin and proud as it sings, steams, and reflects the fire. The raccoon fears it after it catches his paw and seems alive when its cover lifts. Later it duets with the fire during an attack, may spill boiling water on a robber, and ends broken apart on the floor.

records.l: snow, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Snow is light snowfall, fresh, new-fallen, and white. It falls lightly and softly around Toto's cottage, layering the roof, pump, and windows, then covers the ground, heaps into drifts and shapes, and weighs down forest trees in feathery masses.

records.l: winter evening, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A winter evening is cold outside but warm and merry inside the cottage, bringing the group together around the fire for supper, conversation, and a story.

records.l: the supper, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: contains the mutton-pie [exceptionally large and richly filled] The supper includes chicken, ham, a large mutton-pie filled with mutton, eggballs, onions, and rich gravy, along with white and brown bread, jam, gingerbread, apples, nuts, cream, and buttermilk. The guests eat with great enjoyment, while the grandmother listens happily to the sounds of their knives and forks.

records.l: dancing-school, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: teaches dancing [to the family] The dancing-school is held in the kitchen after the story of the Useful Coal, with Toto as instructor and the raccoon, Cracker, and Bruin as dancers. The lesson includes bowing, jumping and changing feet, moving forward and back, balancing, turning partners, and waltzing, but ends in confusion when Bruin destroys the custard pie.

records.l: the grandmother's story, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a story [passed down through two grandmothers] The grandmother's story is introduced as one told to her by her own grandmother. She says that a story passed down through two grandmothers is supposed to be true and begins telling it to the eager group.

records.l: Chop-Chin, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Chop-Chin is a good twelve-year-old boy, Ly-Chee’s son and an apprentice to the Chief Cabinet-maker, who hopes to become a sweeper. When he learns his father must die, he undertakes a sacred mission: he drugs guards and priests, steals the Golden Dragon, enters the royal palace with the Celestial Footstool, hides in the Dragon to command Emperor Wah-Song, and escapes carrying the Footstool.

records.l: Ly-Chee, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Ly-Chee, father of Chop-Chin, is a slightly deaf sweeper who has faithfully kept the Imperial court-yard clean for thirty years to protect the Emperor's passage. He accidentally drenches Emperor Wah-Song with ice-cold water, is condemned and imprisoned, then receives the Golden Dragon's pardon. He gains ducats, jewels, and lifelong appointment as Chief Sweeper, and his family rejoices.

records.l: Emperor Wah-Song, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Emperor Wah-Song, the great and mighty Emperor of China, has a celestial train held up by seven boys and is capricious in going out unannounced. He enters the Imperial court-yard, has Ly-Chee threatened after his clothes are soaked, then mistreats attendants before dreaming of the Golden Dragon. Terrified, he pardons, rewards, and appoints Ly-Chee Chief Sweeper, and becomes meek after his ordeal.

records.l: Tong-Ki-Tcheng, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Tong-Ki-Tcheng, a powerful prince of the Empire, suffers fever in his palace; Chop-Chin invokes his name to gain access to the Golden Dragon.

records.l: the four priests of the First Order of the Saki-Pan, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The four priests of the First Order of the Saki-Pan guard the Golden Dragon, the Jewelled Shrine, and the Temple of the Saki-Pan. They drink wine offered by Chop-Chin and sleep while the idol is removed. Awakening to its disappearance, they fear death, then joyfully return the recovered Dragon to the Temple.

records.l: the Imperial court-yard, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_paved_with white marble [and kept absolutely clean] The Imperial court-yard is a white marble pavement that Ly-Chee and the other sweepers must keep absolutely clean. It is the place where Ly-Chee accidentally drenches the Emperor.

records.l: the great temple of the Golden Dragon, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The great temple of the Golden Dragon is a sacred destination where Chop-Chin arrives at sunset. It has successive guarded courts and includes the Temple of the Golden Dragon. The Golden Dragon is kept on an altar by four priests, who rejoice when returning it after it is found outside.

records.l: the Temple of the Golden Dragon, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The Temple of the Golden Dragon is the House of Gold beyond guarded courts, entered through a golden gate; priests lead Chop-Chin blindfolded to its Jewelled Shrine.

records.l: the Golden Dragon, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The Golden Dragon is the most sacred idol in China, a Fiery Idol worshipped in the Temple of the Saki-Pan. About ten feet long, it stands fifteen feet above the floor on its altar, made of diamond-tipped gold scales, with ruby eyes and an emerald crown. Its faithful servant Ly-Chee brings melons weekly. Chop-Chin steals it from the altar in a crimson sash, then uses it to terrify Emperor Wah-Song into pardoning and rewarding Ly-Chee. Found outside the temple, it is returned by priests, who say it went abroad for the city's welfare.

records.l: the drugged wine, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The drugged wine, sent by Tong-Ki-Tcheng and presented by Chop-Chin, contains a powerful temporary narcotic; guards and priests drink it, sleep deeply, and allow removal of the Golden Dragon.

records.l: the Imperial court-yard accident, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The Imperial court-yard accident occurs when the deaf Ly-Chee throws ice-cold water backward as the Emperor steps outside, drenching his yellow satin clothes and damaging his embroidered shoes.

records.l: Ly-Chee's sentence of death, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Ly-Chee is sentenced by the Emperor to be beheaded at sunrise after soaking the Emperor's clothing and shoes; only the Golden Dragon leaving its altar to beg can revoke the sentence.

records.l: Chop-Chin's mission to the Golden Dragon, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Chop-Chin undertakes a sacred mission to save Ly-Chee, claims prayers for Tong-Ki-Tcheng, uses wine to pass guarded courts, uses a bronze bowl to enter the shrine, and seeks the Golden Dragon's intercession.

records.l: the theft of the Golden Dragon, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The theft of the Golden Dragon is committed by Chop-Chin, who at night climbs its altar, finds the idol surprisingly light, wraps it in his sash, passes sleeping guards and the bronze gate, and escapes into the street.

records.l: the sentinel, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A sentinel at the royal palace’s outer gate, armed with a pike and broadsword, guards the entrance on a dark night, admits Chop-Chin carrying the Celestial Footstool, then lets him leave after a warning against peeping beneath its covering.

records.l: the royal palace, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: has outer gates [closed at night] The royal palace has closed outer gates guarded by a sentinel, though lights remain in many windows. Chop-Chin enters it secretly with the Celestial Footstool and reaches a closet near the Celestial Bed-chamber.

records.l: the Celestial Footstool, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The Celestial Footstool, a sacred object kept covered from profane eyes, is broken when Emperor Wah-Song throws it, repaired by the Chief Cabinet-maker, carried into the palace by Chop-Chin, and used in a false claim of further damage.

records.l: the free pardon for Ly-Chee, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_ordered_by the Golden Dragon [to be sent before day-break] The Golden Dragon commands Emperor Wah-Song to send a free pardon to Ly-Chee before daybreak. The pardon is granted, saving Ly-Chee from execution at sunrise.

records.l: Ly-Chee's appointment as Chief Sweeper, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_ordered_by the Golden Dragon [for life] The Golden Dragon commands that Ly-Chee become Chief Sweeper for life, with gilded brooms, ivory handles, and scrubbing-shoes as yearly benefits. The appointment is carried out, and Ly-Chee is publicly honored in a procession.

records.l: the Dragon's venture from the Temple, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a venture [the Golden Dragon's going out from the Temple] The Dragon's venture from the Temple is discovered when the four priests see that it is missing from the altar. It is later found outside the gate sitting on its hind-legs with its mouth open, and the priests interpret its return as a glorious journey undertaken for the city's welfare.

records.l: the Emperor's dream, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a dreadful dream [in which the Emperor encountered the Golden Dragon] In the Emperor's dream, Wah-Song stands in the Golden Temple before the Jewelled Shrine and hears the Golden Dragon call his name. The Dragon accuses him of condemning Ly-Chee and orders him to pardon and reward the sweeper.

records.l: the Golden Dragon's command, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The Golden Dragon commands Emperor Wah-Song to pardon and reward Ly-Chee and appoint sweepers; terrified by threats, the Emperor agrees.

records.l: the cellar, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The cellar, beneath a cottage, contains brown mice and is home to Squeak, Scrabble, and their mother. After a frightening kitchen adventure, the young mice return there, while someone seeks to remove the troublesome, thieving mice without killing them.

records.l: squash pie, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Squash pie is lovely and especially fine; after a remaining piece is left at dinner, two brown mice find it in the cupboard and eat it completely, leaving the plate white and empty.

records.l: Squeak, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a mouse [little and brown] Squeak enters the kitchen with Scrabble, helps enlarge the cupboard crack, and eats squash pie and hot ginger. After cooling off in a basin, Squeak climbs Bruin, mistakes him for a hill, and flees when he moves.

records.l: Scrabble, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a mouse [little and brown] Scrabble enters the kitchen with Squeak and helps eat the squash pie and ginger. Scrabble climbs Bruin, whom the mice mistake for a black hill, and escapes with Squeak after Bruin shakes himself.

records.l: the mice, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: live_in the cellar [normally] The mice are Squeak and Scrabble, two little brown mice who live in a cellar. They sneak into the kitchen, eat pie and ginger, suffer from the ginger's heat, cool themselves in water, and flee back home after mistaking Bruin for a moving hill.

records.l: the mice's kitchen adventure, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: involves squash pie The mice's kitchen adventure begins when Squeak and Scrabble enter through a crack under the cellar-door to explore and find food. They eat squash pie, accidentally eat hot ginger, cool themselves in a basin, and then climb onto Bruin before fleeing in terror.

records.l: the mice's encounter with Bruin, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_caused_by Bruin [while he sleeps on the hearth-rug] The mice mistake the sleeping Bruin for a vast black hill and climb over him. When Bruin stretches, shakes, yawns, and opens his mouth, the mice imagine that they have seen a fiery cavern and rush back to the cellar.

records.l: woodmouse, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A small brown woodland mouse, distantly related to brown mice, meets <DW53> and Toto on a winter walk, discusses forest room, and invites them to his son Prick-ear’s wedding.

records.l: Prick-ear, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Prick-ear, the woodmouse's eldest son and bridegroom, begins resenting the raccoon for eating his checkerberries and chasing him, then greets and presents him as a friend at his cave wedding.

records.l: brown mice, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Two brown mice live in the cottage cellar, troubling and damaging it; they enter at night, gobble squash pie, flee, and are to be sent to the forest.

records.l: the woodmouse family wedding, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The woodmouse family wedding takes place in the cave on the second evening after the meeting, with many relatives and invited guests <DW53> and Toto.

records.l: winter walk, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: takes_place_in the forest [through fresh snow] <DW53> and Toto take a winter walk from the yard toward the forest after the sky clears. They travel through fresh snow, recall earlier events, and meet the woodmouse.

records.l: the forest, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The forest is a wild home and beloved woodland place for Toto, the party of friends, brown mice, and many small creatures. It contains Chucky's aunt's burrow, a hollow tree, and a fairy pool. In fresh snow it shows creatures' tracks and homes and offers the brown mice space for a new home. In spring it calls wild creatures back; Toto, Bruin, and the grandmother return to enjoy its pool, greenery, water, birds, and insects.

records.l: the cave, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A large, low cave is engaged for the woodmouse family's wedding because it can hold their relatives. Its bramble-cleared entrance is flanked by light-wood torches; inside, glow-worms and torches provide light, while holly and alder branches decorate the floor, walls, and corners for festivity.

records.l: Pigeon Pretty, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Pigeon Pretty is a sober-minded wood-pigeon and the grandmother’s companion, perching on her shoulder during a dancing lesson. She affectionately reassures Bruin about his size. Later, anticipating Baldhead’s fear of Bruin, she brings reviving dried leaves, restores the fainted hermit, and explains Bruin’s kindness so he can welcome the visitors.

records.l: King Sligo, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: King Sligo is a rich, kind-hearted king ruling his kingdom. After repeated treasure thefts, he follows the Useful Coal's instructions, exposes the High Cellarer, and sets the coal in sapphires on his crown.

records.l: High Cellarer, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The High Cellarer, an officer of the king, secretly steals King Sligo's treasure while feigning investigation; the Useful Coal thwarts him twice, exposes his blackened hands, and leads to his arrest and beheading.

records.l: the Useful Coal, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The Useful Coal, a speaking, sentient coal, promises to save King Sligo's treasure three times and identify its thief. Burning black and red, it burns and frightens the High Cellarer, reveals him with soot, then dies and becomes a black diamond in the king's crown.

records.l: treasure-chamber, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A royal chamber holding gold, jewels, and sapphires, protected by King Sligo’s key; the High Cellarer finds the key, enters, steals treasure, and locks the chamber before facing the king.

records.l: the theft of the king's treasure, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_committed_by High Cellarer The theft of the king's treasure is carried out by the High Cellarer, who repeatedly uses his position to steal gold and jewels. King Sligo stops the theft through the Useful Coal's plan, identifies the culprit by his blackened hands, and finds stolen sapphires and the treasure-chamber key on him.

records.l: the story of the Useful Coal, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_told_by raccoon [to the family around the fire] The story of the Useful Coal concerns King Sligo's efforts to discover who is stealing his treasure. The coal protects the king's property three times, reveals the High Cellarer as the thief, and is rewarded by being made into a black diamond in the king's crown.

records.l: the wedding of the woodmouse's eldest son, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The woodmouse's eldest son's wedding occurs in a decorated cave, gathers woodland creatures and the woodmouse's daughters, includes a marriage ceremony, feast, and dancing, then ends.

records.l: woodmouse's bride, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a mouse [pretty and wearing a brown-fur travelling-dress] The woodmouse's bride is a pretty little mouse wearing a becoming brown-fur travelling dress. She is frightened by the arrival of the raccoon and Toto but takes part in the ceremony and leaves with her husband for their new home.

records.l: Mr. Woodmouse, Senior, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_father_of woodmouse's eldest son Mr. Woodmouse, Senior, welcomes Toto, Cracker, and the raccoon despite the alarm they cause among the guests. He explains the raccoon's earlier trouble with his son and is relieved when Toto assures him that the raccoon now feels kindly toward the family.

records.l: little woodmice, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Little woodmice, numerous wedding guests and good people, fear Toto and the raccoon, then recover, dance and feast, make checkerberries and nuts for Toto, and send Bruin regretful apologies.

records.l: the wedding party, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The wedding party gathers woodmice, field-mice, kangaroo-mice, moles, squirrels, Titmice, Mrs. Shrew and her daughters, and other small creatures. Toto and the raccoon briefly frighten the guests; afterward, they resume greeting, dancing, eating, and drinking.

records.l: the marriage ceremony, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A distinguished star-nosed mole officiant performs a marriage ceremony: bride and groom eat wintergreen leaves, nibble a third together, and rub noses when they meet in the middle.

records.l: the wedding feast, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The wedding feast offers nuts, acorns, berries, wintergreen leaves, sassafras-bark, spruce-gum, golden corn, and root-beer in edible birch-bark goblets; guests drink and eat, while star-nosed moles overeat until their stars turn purple.

records.l: the dancing, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_accompanied_by Toto's whistle [a jig and later a waltz] Toto's whistle leads the wedding party in jigs and waltzes. Cracker dances with a young red squirrel, while Toto and the raccoon perform a waltz admired by the guests; the celebration ends after one final wild dance.

records.l: comet, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A comet is a heavenly body with a head and shining tail among the constellations. It travels the sky at great speed, though motion may be unseen, disappears, and sometimes returns only after a thousand years.

records.l: The Naughty Comet, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a story [about comets and disobedience] The Naughty Comet is the story of Short-Tail Comet No. 73, who becomes curious about why comets travel and disobeys the Comet Master's orders. Its disobedience leads to No. 73 being devoured by the Sun, and the story is presented as a warning to the other comets.

records.l: Comet Master, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Comet Master is master of the comets, directing their assigned journeys and restrictions. Carrying a very long, sharp-pointed stick, he prods and punishes comets that misbehave. He sends Short-Tail Comet No. 73 on a thirteen-week, three-day journey with prohibitions, then orders No. 1 Express to find a runaway meteor and take it to planet Bungo.

records.l: Short-Tail Comet No. 73, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A young, short-tailed comet assigned a thirteen-week journey seeks why comets travel, disobeys the Comet Master by speaking to a meteor and approaching the Sun, and is devoured.

records.l: meteor, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Meteor defies the Comet Master, persuades Short-Tail Comet No. 73 to travel toward the Sun, flees after No. 73 is devoured, and is ordered arrested and taken to Bungo.

records.l: the sun, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The Sun attracts and devours Short-Tail Comet No. 73, making it travel faster and burn, then is replaced by the moon at night.

records.l: the moon, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The moon, a shining silver globe in the sky, rises after sunset; a young cow mistakes a voice for Bossy’s, leaps toward it, and disappears.

records.l: Mr. Baldhead, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Mr. Baldhead is an old hermit from Ireland who lives in Baldhead’s cave with a broken, lame leg. Weak, pale, and nearly starving after more than a week confined without food, he begins to recover when water and food arrive. Though he first faints at Bruin’s presence, he welcomes the bear after learning of his charitable mission. He plays Russian backgammon with Bruin, owns and reads books for amusement, shelters Ger-Falcon for winter, and tells Toto, Bruin, and Pigeon Pretty an Irish fairy story.

records.l: Jim Crow, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Jim Crow is Baldhead's faithful, lame crow companion. Sick and unable to find food, he regains strength after Bruin gives him roast chicken, then leads Bruin and Toto to Baldhead's cave and laughs with them. Later, as Toto's guest, he politely introduces himself at the cottage and escorts Miss Mary indoors.

records.l: the forest, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The forest is a place of deep woods, ferns, mosses, and a spider’s web, containing the Green Man’s oak-tree and toadstool. Eileen gathers sticks there, encounters the tiny Green Man, escapes the doctor’s house into it, and carefully travels to the oak tree and toadstool.

records.l: Baldhead's cave, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A lonely cave dwelling with a rustic porch shelters helpless Baldhead, who lies on a rough pallet beneath dim roof-hole light.

records.l: Baldhead's broken leg, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a injury Baldhead's broken leg has left him unable to move for more than a week. Bruin and Toto bring bandages and medicines intended to help care for it.

records.l: aid for Baldhead, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Aid for Baldhead brings nourishing food, medicines, bandages, and water to his cave, where Bruin and Toto deliver care for his broken leg.

records.l: food, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_intended_for Baldhead [as nourishment during his illness] Food is urgently needed because Baldhead has none in his cave and is close to starving. Bruin brings a basket of provisions, feeds Jim Crow a roast-chicken wing, and provides Baldhead with water, jelly, and other nourishing food.

records.l: robber, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: An ill-looking thief with a hooked nose, straggling red beard, and green eyes, he enters a cottage with a heavy robber's pack, steals food and searches for valuables, threatens Miss Mary, then is attacked by a raccoon and scalded, fleeing screaming down the road.

records.l: robbery and attack, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A robbery and attack unfolds in a cottage when a robber steals food and tries to take silver teaspoons and a porringer. Miss Mary exposes him; Bruin attacks with teeth and claws, and a kettle pours boiling water on his legs. He escapes, after which Miss Mary and Bruin reconcile and thank each other.

records.l: the attempted robbery of Toto's chickens, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: targets the Black Spanish chickens [attempted by Ger-Falcon] Ger-Falcon admits that he tried to carry off Toto's Black Spanish chickens because he was starving. Toto says that people eat their own chickens but do not steal other people's chickens.

records.l: the hermit's cave, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The hermit's cave houses the recovering hermit and Bruin, hosts visitors and backgammon, and becomes winter refuge where Ger-Falcon is fed and sheltered.

records.l: the moon-calf, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a calf [said to live in the moon] The moon-calf is described as a calf believed by the young cow to live in the moon. The young cow thinks Bossy has become a moon-calf after hearing the phrase from the maid and the Oldest Ox.

records.l: the young cow, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The young cow, mother of and very fond of Bossy, grieves when her calf is taken away, believes he is on the moon, leaps toward it, overshoots it, and vanishes forever.

records.l: Bossy, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Bossy, the young cow's missing calf, is believed by her to live as a moon-calf; she calls to him while trying to reach the moon.

records.l: The Three Remarks, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a story The Three Remarks is the story Miss Mary tells about a princess who can reply only with three fixed phrases. The phrases are “What is the price of butter?”, “Has your grandmother sold her mangle yet?”, and “With all my heart!”

records.l: princess, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The princess is beautiful, wise, graceful, and gentle, with black hair and star-like eyes, but can make only three remarks. Pressured by her father to accept a marriage proposal, she leaves to avoid it. Her fixed replies help her expose or outwit a butterman impostor and robbers, gaining rubies and sapphires. She finally accepts marriage with the young king she loves.

records.l: butterman impostor, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The butterman impostor, a retired butterman, claims an empty throne, is accepted and rules as king, carries a sceptre, then mistakes the princess’s butter question for recognition, pays her six thousand rubies for silence, and leaves the throne.

records.l: city, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: After the late king dies heirless, the city prepares and accepts the butterman impostor as king, then lets him leave and cheers the departing princess.

records.l: robbers, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A heavily armed, forest-dwelling band of robbers stops a princess, questions her and her bag, mistakes her mangle remark for a countersign, takes her to its chief, and gives her ten thousand sapphires for secrecy.

records.l: Red Chief of the Rustywhanger, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The gigantic robber chieftain leads Red Chief's band, hides a bag of sapphires in an oak, mistakes a princess's remark for an approaching enemy army, and offers her sapphires and escape.

records.l: Eileen's escape, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Eileen’s escape begins when Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy leaves and she puts Mrs. O'Shaughnessy to sleep with a monotonous story. She runs across fields into a deep forest, meets robbers after encountering the Red Chief of the Rustywhanger, then follows a ferny path toward open country and the Green Man.

records.l: young king, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Young king rules from a marble and jasper palace, rides out with his court to catch nighthawks, falls in love with the princess, and proposes; she gladly accepts.

records.l: marriage, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_between young king [and princess] Marriage proposals are a recurring problem for the princess because she can answer them only with one of her three remarks. She refuses to accept any suitor until she meets the young king, whose proposal she gladly accepts.

records.l: bag of rubies, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: contains rubies [six thousand rubies] The butterman impostor gives the princess a bag of rubies containing six thousand gems, each as large as a pigeon's egg, in exchange for her silence about his identity.

records.l: rubies, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The rubies are offered by the butterman impostor as a bribe to prevent his exposure. Later, the princess gives one ruby to the young king to show that she is not a beggar.

records.l: bag of sapphires, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: contains sapphires [ten thousand sapphires] The Red Chief of the Rustywhanger gives the princess a bag of sapphires containing ten thousand gems, each as large as a pullet's egg, so that she will follow the route he indicates and not betray his band.

records.l: sapphires, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The sapphires are the payment offered by the Red Chief of the Rustywhanger to secure the princess's cooperation. Later, the princess gives one sapphire to the young king along with a ruby.

records.l: the crow, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The crow, the hermit's companion, learns backgammon but cannot lift the dice-box and upsets pieces; afraid of Ger-Falcon, he hides until Toto reassures him.

records.l: Ger-Falcon, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Ger-Falcon, a wild, lawless hawk and hunted forest outlaw, is the family's present representative, descended from its grandfather seventy times removed. Starving, he pursues Pigeon Pretty; Bruin captures him. After broth, he recounts royal service and stays with the hermit through snow and frost.

records.l: the winter, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A season especially difficult for Ger-Falcon: it prevents respectable ordinary living; he goes a week without food until the hermit offers feeding until snow and frost pass.

records.l: the hawk's pursuit of Pigeon Pretty, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_caused_by Ger-Falcon's hunger [after a week without food] Ger-Falcon chases Pigeon Pretty into the hermit's cave, where she is exhausted and falls fainting at Bruin's feet. Bruin captures the hawk before he can pounce on her.

records.l: the Ger-Falcon family, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a old and honorable race [despite being wild and lawless] The Ger-Falcon family was once trained to pursue, overtake, and kill for the hunting sports of men. Ger-Falcon says that one ancestor served an emperor, but after fashion changed and hawking declined, the family became hunted outlaws dependent on barn-yards and hen-roosts.

records.l: the fairy story, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_about the fairy-folk [an Irish story] The hermit agrees to tell an Irish fairy story after Toto asks for a tale about fairies. He says that he lived in Ireland as a boy, which he calls the very home of the fairy-folk.

records.l: Eileen Macarthy, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Eileen Macarthy is a girl of the Macarthy family who lives in the Macarthy cottage with her parents, Honor and Dennis, and her brother Phelim, whom she cares for. A talkative child who loves talking and knows many fairy stories, she pities a grasshopper and later goes into the forest to gather sticks for her mother. There she frees a tiny Green Man from a spider’s web and receives a wish: whenever she speaks, diamonds and pearls fall from her mouth. After she crosses her home’s threshold, the jewels alarm her family. Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy takes her from her parents and holds her prisoner, forcing her to speak continually in his house. Eileen escapes the O'Shaughnessy house by telling Mrs. O'Shaughnessy a long story until she sleeps. She returns to the Green Man and asks that the charm be removed, then goes home with pearls and diamonds in her apron. Her account is believed; she grows into a good, rich woman and marries the young Count of Kilmoggan.

records.l: the Green Men, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The Green Men are fairies and woodland people who live in the forest. A tiny Green Man, wearing a light green jacket and scarlet cap, grants Eileen Macarthy a wish after she saves him from a spider’s web and sends her good wishes. Later, the Green Men pursue Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy in sport and revenge around County Kerry three times for thrice three days, then let him collapse in a bog and vanish.

records.l: Honor Macarthy, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Honor Macarthy, Eileen Macarthy’s physically strong mother, anxiously awaits Eileen, mistakes diamonds and pearls falling from her mouth for bewitchment, silences her, and defends her against accusations of stealing the Countess’s jewels.

records.l: Dennis Macarthy, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_a father [of Eileen Macarthy] Dennis Macarthy comes to the cottage after Phelim calls him and examines the shining objects. He first believes Eileen has swallowed or stolen the Countess’s jewels, then asks Dr. O’Shaughnessy whether Eileen can be cured at home before reluctantly allowing the doctor to take her.

records.l: Phelim Macarthy, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Phelim Macarthy is a boy in the Macarthy family, son of Dennis and little brother of Eileen. He and Eileen share a trundle-bed, and he depends on her at night. He sees shining objects and calls them marbles, runs for Dennis, and stops Dr. O’Shaughnessy’s carriage so Eileen can be examined and taken away.

records.l: Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy is a local physician, married to Mrs. O'Shaughnessy, who lives in the doctor's house and owns a narrow gig and old pony. He examines Eileen Macarthy and the supposed diamonds and pearls, dismissing them as glass and trash, judges her seriously ill, and takes her home to attempt an experiment as a cure. He then holds Eileen captive, intending that she speak jewels until his best room is full. Driven by greed, he imagines becoming King Michael and claiming Ireland's crown for wealth, power, and royal glory. When Eily disappears and the jewels become reptiles, his ambition collapses: he flees and is pursued by the Green Men across County Kerry for three times three days, finally falling exhausted into a bog.

records.l: Mrs. O'Shaughnessy, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Mrs. O'Shaughnessy, Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy's wife, helps guard Eileen Macarthy on her husband's order and greedily gathers diamonds and pearls. Left alone with Eileen on the third day, she falls asleep during Eileen's tedious story, enabling Eileen's escape. She raises the alarm, blames witches, and is violently reproached by her husband.

records.l: the Macarthy cottage, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The Macarthy cottage is the family’s small home, containing the kitchen, hall, dining-room, and drawing-room. Eileen crosses its threshold before the charm takes effect, and the diamonds and pearls roll across its floor as her family reacts with alarm.

records.l: the fairy wish, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The fairy wish Eileen chose is a charm that makes diamonds and pearls appear whenever she speaks. The Green Man warns she may want it removed and gives a holly-and-toadstool ritual. Later, he touches her lips with his cap and declares the charm off.

records.l: the diamonds and pearls curse, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The diamonds and pearls curse makes a diamond and a pearl fall from Eileen’s mouth whenever she speaks. Her family takes the jewels as stolen or bewitched, and Dr. Michael O’Shaughnessy calls them glass and removes her for treatment. Though the fairy’s gift brings misery through his exploitation, it leads to the lesson that loving words and helpful deeds are greater treasures. If Eileen wishes, the spell reversal ritual can remove it.

records.l: the Green Man's toadstool, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The Green Man's toadstool is a large forest plant at the foot of the Green Man's oak-tree and serves as his seat. When Eileen seeks to remove a charm, she returns there with a sprig of holly, taps or strikes it three times, and speaks the reversal words, causing the Green Man to appear.

records.l: the Green Man, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The Green Man is a dwindling supernatural fairy at a toadstool beneath an oak-tree. He gives Eileen Macarthy a wish causing diamonds and pearls to fall from her lips, then removes the charm when she returns and teaches that gentle words are pearls and kind deeds diamonds.

records.l: diamonds and pearls, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Pearls and diamonds are jewels produced whenever Eileen speaks. They fill her lap, the floor, and by the third day the best room to ankle depth, but vanish before Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy sees them. Eily later carries them home in her apron; the Green Man says kind words and deeds are better jewels.

records.l: the O'Shaughnessy house, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The O'Shaughnessy house is a tall, dark, gloomy house with greenish window-panes and gaunt chimneys. Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy brings Eileen there and guards her; Eily is held captive there. After Eily disappears, reptiles pursue the doctor through its passage and out.

records.l: the best room, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: contains Eileen's imprisonment [the room where Eileen is confined] The best room is a large, bare room where Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy confines Eileen and orders her to talk until it is full. After several days, it becomes covered with diamonds and pearls.

records.l: Eileen's imprisonment, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: takes_place_in the best room [at the doctor's house] Eileen's imprisonment lasts three days in the doctor's best room, where she must talk almost continuously while Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy and Mrs. O'Shaughnessy guard her. She is threatened with a birch rod when she refuses to continue speaking.

records.l: the wish to become King of Ireland, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_denied Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy [the Green Man says he has already received his kingdom] Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy intends to use Eileen's diamonds and pearls to become King of Ireland, and he says he may become rich enough to buy Ireland and England. The Green Man assures Eileen that Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy will not become King of Ireland, though he says the doctor has come into his kingdom by then.

records.l: the reptiles, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Reptiles include toads, snakes, and newts; they cover the floor where jewels had been, then hop, creep, and wriggle through an open door, pursuing Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy out.

records.l: Eily's disappearance, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_attributed_to the witches [by Mrs. O'Shaughnessy] Mrs. O'Shaughnessy discovers that Eily is gone and believes witches have taken her up the chimney. The disappearance is followed by the transformation of the jewels into reptiles, while Eily is later revealed to have gone home with pearls and diamonds.

records.l: the pursuit of Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_conducted_by the Green Men [in sport and revenge] After Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy flees the house, the reptiles pursue him over hills, dales, moss, and moor. The Green Men continue the hunt around County Kerry until he drops exhausted in a bog.

records.l: royal glory and kingship, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy dreams of becoming King Michael and imagines Queen Victory welcoming him to her throne. He plans to ask her for the loan of her Sunday crown as a pattern, but his royal meditations end when Mrs. O'Shaughnessy announces Eily's disappearance.

records.l: the old hermit, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: An old, forest-dwelling hermit lives lonely in a cavern with a crow and hawk. He arrives at a party bearing both birds and announces melting snow, warmer sun, and approaching spring.

records.l: the party, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: A real party at the cottage gathers friends including Toto, the grandmother, Bruin, the raccoon, the old hermit, Chucky, Jim Crow, Ger-Falcon, and birds. They eat, tell stories, play old-fashioned games, and dance to Toto’s fiddle at their merriest, final gathering.

records.l: spring, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_approaching the forest [snow melting and weather mild] Spring is said to be approaching because the snow is melting, the sun is warmer, and the air is mild. The prospect excites the forest animals but makes Toto and Bruin uneasy because it signals that their time together is ending.

records.l: eggs, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: are_used_for the custard [fresh eggs gathered from the hens] Toto gathers fresh eggs from Mrs. Speckle and Dame Clucket for the party’s custard. The hens reluctantly give them to him because they are soft-hearted and Toto has not had eggs for several days.

records.l: the little cottage, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: The little cottage, home to Toto, the blind grandmother, and later Bruin, hosts spring farewells, Bruin’s secret stay, and laughing forest-friend visits.

records.l: departure for the forest, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: In spring, the woodchuck, squirrel, wood-pigeon, raccoon, and Toto leave the cottage for the forest, looking back and waving; Bruin stays behind, intending to remain with Toto and the blind grandmother.

records.l: farewell, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: is_exchanged_between the party of friends [at the cottage door] The farewell is affectionate and sorrowful as the animals thank the blind grandmother and promise to visit her in the forest or return to the cottage. The blind grandmother says good-by to each friend, but Bruin avoids the farewell because he cannot say that he is leaving. When he is brought back, the group replaces the painful farewell with a promise that he will never leave them.

records.l: life at the cottage, Toto's Merry Winter
records.s: Life at the cottage continues happily after the other animals return to the forest. Bruin settles permanently and performs household and farm work, while Toto, the blind grandmother, and forest friends spend afternoons together and share laughing stories each evening.

1.  Burzee

Have you heard of the great Forest of Burzee?  Nurse used to sing of it
when I was a child.  She sang of the big tree-trunks, standing close
together, with their roots intertwining below the earth and their
branches intertwining above it; of their rough coating of bark and
queer, gnarled limbs; of the bushy foliage that roofed the entire
forest, save where the sunbeams found a path through which to touch the
ground in little spots and to cast weird and curious shadows over the
mosses, the lichens and the drifts of dried leaves.

The Forest of Burzee is mighty and grand and awesome to those who steal
beneath its shade.  Coming from the sunlit meadows into its mazes it
seems at first gloomy, then pleasant, and afterward filled with
never-ending delights.

For hundreds of years it has flourished in all its magnificence,

records.l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, YOUTH / 1. Burzee
records.s: seems at first gloomy, then pleasant, and afterward filled with never-ending delights. For hundreds of years it has flourished in all its magnificence, the silence of its inclosure unbroken save by the chirp of busy chipmunks, the growl of wild beasts and the songs of birds. Yet Burzee has its inhabitants--for all this. Nature peopled it in the beginning with Fairies, Knooks, Ryls and Nymphs. As long as the Forest stands it will be a home, a refuge and a playground to these sweet immortals, who revel undisturbed in its depths. Civilization has never yet reached Burzee. 2.  The Child of the Forest

Once, so long ago our great-grandfathers could scarcely have heard it
mentioned, there lived within the great Forest of Burzee a wood-nymph
named Necile.  She was closely related to the mighty Queen Zurline, and
her home was beneath the shade of a widespreading oak.  Once every
year, on Budding Day, when the trees put forth their new buds, Necile
held the Golden Chalice of

Once every year, on Budding Day, when the trees put forth their new buds, Necile held the Golden Chalice of Ak to the lips of the Queen, who drank therefrom to the prosperity of the Forest. So you see she was a nymph of some importance, and, moreover, it is said she was highly regarded because of her beauty and grace. When she was created she could not have told; Queen Zurline could not have told; the great Ak himself could not have told. It was long ago when the world was new and nymphs were needed to guard the forests and to minister to the wants of the young trees. Then, on some day not remembered, Necile sprang into being; radiant, lovely, straight and slim as the sapling she was created to guard. Her hair was the color that lines a chestnut-bur; her eyes were blue in the sunlight and purple in the shade; her cheeks bloomed with the faint pink that edges the clouds at sunset; her lips were full red, pouting and sweet. Yet suffering, in moderation, is the natural lot of mortals, and it is not our place to interfere with the laws of Nature." Taking Claus to a small clearing in the forest, the Master said: "Place

records.l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. Claus Discovers Humanity
records.s: said: "Place your hand upon my girdle and hold fast while we journey through the air; for now shall we encircle the world and look upon many of the haunts of those men from whom you are descended." These words caused Claus to marvel, for until now he had thought himself the only one of his kind upon the earth; yet in silence he grasped firmly the girdle of the great Ak, his astonishment forbidding speech. Then the vast forest of Burzee seemed to fall away from their feet, and the youth found himself passing swiftly through the air at a great height. Ere long there were spires beneath them, while buildings of many shapes and colors met their downward view. It was a city of men, and Ak, pausing to descend, led Claus to its inclosure. Said the Master: "So long as you hold fast to my girdle you will remain unseen by all mankind, though seeing clearly yourself. To release your grasp will be to separate yourself forever from me and your home in Burzee." One of the first laws of the Forest is obedience, and Claus had no thought of disobeying the Master's wish.

"Indeed," said Ak, "the immortals are few; but the mortals are many." Claus looked earnestly upon his fellows. Some worked at tedious tasks; some strutted in impudent conceit; some were thoughtful and grave while others seemed happy and content. Men of many natures were there, as everywhere, and Claus found much to please him and much to make him sad. But especially he noted the children--first curiously, then eagerly, then lovingly. Thereafter with each moment passed in the city the youth's wonder grew.
He, who had supposed himself created differently from all others, now
found the earth swarming with creatures of his own kind.

"Indeed," said Ak, "the immortals are few; but the mortals are many."

Claus looked earnestly upon his fellows.  There were sad faces, gay and
reckless faces, pleasant faces, anxious faces and kindly faces, all
mingled in puzzling disorder.  Some worked at tedious tasks; some
strutted in impudent conceit; some were thoughtful and grave while
others seemed happy and content.  Men of many natures were there, as
everywhere, and Claus found much to please him and much to make him sad.

Claus understood, and turning to the Forest's edge he selected a number of fallen tree-trunks, which he began to clear of their dead branches. He would not cut into a living tree. His life among the nymphs who guarded the Forest had taught him that a live tree is sacred, being a created thing endowed with feeling. But with the dead and fallen trees it was different. They had fulfilled their destiny, as active members of the Forest community, and now it was fitting that their remains should minister to the needs of man. The ax bit deep into the logs at every stroke. It seemed to have a force of its own, and Claus had but to swing and guide it. When shadows began creeping over the green hills to lie in the Valley overnight, the young man had chopped many logs into equal lengths and proper shapes for building a house such as he had seen the poorer classes of men inhabit. Friendships are not easily broken, and the immortals are everywhere.

Upon reaching the brook he drank of the pure water, and then sat down
on the bank to laugh at the mischievous gambols of the ripples as they
pushed one another against rocks or crowded desperately to see which
should first reach the turn beyond.  And as they raced away he listened
to the song they sang:

2.  How Claus Made the First Toy

Truly our Claus had wisdom, for his good fortune but strengthened his
resolve to befriend the little ones of his own race.  He knew his plan
was approved by the immortals, else they would not have favored him so
greatly.

So he began at once to make acquaintance with mankind.  He walked
through the Valley to the plain beyond, and crossed the plain in many
directions to reach the abodes of men.  These stood singly or

records.l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. How Claus Made the First Toy
records.s: walked through the Valley to the plain beyond, and crossed the plain in many directions to reach the abodes of men. These stood singly or in groups of dwellings called villages, and in nearly all the houses, whether big or little, Claus found children. The youngsters soon came to know his merry, laughing face and the kind glance of his bright eyes; and the parents, while they regarded the young man with some scorn for loving children more than their elders, were content that the girls and boys had found a playfellow who seemed willing to amuse them. So the children romped and played games with Claus, and the boys rode upon his shoulders, and the girls nestled in his strong arms, and the babies clung fondly to his knees. Wherever the young man chanced to be, the sound of childish laughter followed him; and to understand this better you must know that children were much neglected in those days and received little attention from their parents, so that it became to them a marvel that so goodly a man as Claus devoted his time to making them happy. dimpled with smiles as she started along the path toward home.

Claus thanked the Master Woodsman most gratefully and returned to his Valley, while Ak, who never delayed carrying out his promises, at once traveled to the mountains of the Awgwas. There, standing on the bare rocks, he called on the King and his people to appear. Instantly the place was filled with throngs of the scowling Awgwas, and their King, perching himself on a point of rock, demanded fiercely: "Who dares call on us?" And joined to these were the Goozzle-Goblins, with long talons as sharp as swords, with which they clawed the flesh from their foes. The First Journey with the Reindeer Those were happy days for Claus when he carried his accumulation of toys to the children who had awaited them so long. During his imprisonment in the Valley he had been so industrious that all his shelves were filled with playthings, and after quickly supplying the little ones living near by he saw he must now extend his travels to wider fields. Remembering the time when he had journeyed with Ak through all the world, he knew children were everywhere, and he longed to make as many as possible happy with his gifts. So he loaded a great sack with all kinds of toys, slung it upon his back that he might carry it more easily, and started off on a longer trip than he had yet undertaken. Wherever he showed his merry face, in hamlet or in farmhouse, he received a cordial welcome, for his fame had spread into far lands. At each village the children swarmed about him, following his footsteps wherever he went; and the women thanked him gratefully for the joy he brought their little

8.  The First Journey with the Reindeer

Those were happy days for Claus when he carried his accumulation of
toys to the children who had awaited them so long.  During his
imprisonment in the Valley he had been so industrious that all his
shelves were filled with playthings, and after quickly supplying the
little ones living near by he saw he must now extend his travels to
wider fields.

Remembering the time when he had journeyed with Ak through all the
world, he knew children were everywhere, and he longed to make as many
as possible happy with his gifts.

So he loaded a great sack with all kinds of toys, slung it upon his
back that he might carry it more easily, and started off on a longer
trip than he had yet undertaken.

Wherever he showed his merry face, in hamlet or in farmhouse, he
received a cordial welcome, for his fame had spread into far lands.  At
each village the children swarmed about him, following his footsteps
wherever he went; and the women thanked him gratefully for the joy he
brought their little

records.l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
records.s: the children swarmed about him, following his footsteps wherever he went; and the women thanked him gratefully for the joy he brought their little ones; and the men looked upon him curiously that he should devote his time to such a queer occupation as toy-making. But every one smiled on him and gave him kindly words, and Claus felt amply repaid for his long journey. When the sack was empty he went back again to the Laughing Valley and once more filled it to the brim. This time he followed another road, into a different part of the country, and carried happiness to many children who never before had owned a toy or guessed that such a delightful plaything existed. After a third journey, so far away that Claus was many days walking the distance, the store of toys became exhausted and without delay he set about making a fresh supply. From seeing so many children and studying their tastes he had acquired several new ideas about toys. The dollies were, he had found, the most delightful of all playthings for babies and little girls, and often those who could not say "dolly" would call for a "doll" in their sweet baby talk. So

records.s: So Glossie and Flossie went to the Forest to choose their mates, and Claus began to consider the question of a harness for them all. In the end he called upon Peter Knook for assistance, for Peter's heart is as kind as his body is crooked, and he is remarkably shrewd, as well. And now we come to a turning-point in the career of Santa Claus, and it
is my duty to relate the most remarkable that has happened since the
world began or mankind was created.

helpless infant by the Wood-Nymph Necile and reared to manhood in the
great Forest of Burzee.  And we know how he began to make toys for
children and how, with the assistance and goodwill of the immortals, he
was able to distribute them to the little ones throughout the world.

hard-working life he led gave him perfect health and strength.  And
doubtless a man can live longer in the beautiful Laughing Valley, where

Then all the Forest of Burzee became sad and all the Laughing Valley was hushed; for every living thing that had known Claus had used to love him and to brighten at the sound of his footsteps or the notes of his merry whistle. No doubt the old man's strength was at last exhausted, for he made no more toys, but lay on his bed as in a dream. He sprang from his bed and stood where the bright sunshine came in through his window and flooded him with its merry, dancing rays. records.l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. When the World Grew Old
records.s: were so greatly interested in his labors that they gladly rendered him their assistance. Ak gave him his man Kilter, "the silent and swift." And the Knook Prince gave him Peter, who was more crooked and less surly than any of his brothers. And the Ryl Prince gave him Nuter, the sweetest tempered Ryl ever known. records.s: merry within. The snow was falling lightly, softly, with no gusts of wind to trouble it and send it whirling and drifting hither and thither. It covered the roof with a smooth white counterpane, tucking it in neatly and carefully round the edges; it put a tall conical cap on top of the pump, and laid an ermine fold over his long and impressive nose. Myriads of curious little flakes pattered softly--oh! very softly--against the windows of the cottage, pressing against the glass to see what was going on inside, and saying, "Let us in! let us in! please do!" But nobody seemed inclined to let them in, so they were forced to content themselves with looking. Indeed, the aspect of the kitchen was very inviting, and it is no wonder that the little cold flakes wanted to get in. A great fire was crackling and leaping on the hearth. The whole room seemed to glow and glitter: brass saucepans, tin platters, glass window-panes, all cast their very brightest glances toward the fire, to show him that they appreciated his efforts. On the hob beside the fire sat the tea-kettle, a brilliant contrast to its sooty neighbor. It was of copper, so brightly burnished that it shone like the good red gold. records.s: make a good cheerful noise, and not so hard as to boil all the water away. And _why_ that beast should sit and glower at me there as he is doing, is more than I can understand." "That beast" was a raccoon. I think some of you children may have seen him before. He was sitting in front of the fire, with his beautiful tail curled comfortably about his toes; and he certainly _was_ staring very hard at the tea-kettle. Presently the kettle, in pure playfulness and good-will, lifted its cover a little and let out an extra puff of snowy steam; and at that the raccoon gave a jump, and moved farther away from the fire, without ever taking his eyes off the kettle. The fact is, that for the first time in his life the raccoon knew what _fear_ was. He was afraid--mortally afraid--of that tea-kettle. "Don't tell me!" he had said to Toto, only the day before, "don't tell _me_ it isn't alive! It breathes, and it talks, and it moves, and if that isn't being alive I don't know what is." "<DW53>, how utterly absurd you are!" cried Toto, laughing.

"I have been splitting kindling-wood," said Toto, "and building a snow fort, and snowballing Bruin. And he has--" "I have been talking to the pig," said Bruin, very gravely. "The pig. Yes. He is a very singular animal, that pig. Is it true," he added, turning to Toto, "that he has never left that place, that sty, since he was born?" "Never, except to go into the yard by the cow-shed," said Toto. "His sty opens into the yard, you know. But I don't think he cares to go out often." "That is what he said," rejoined the bear. The bear washed and cooked, churned and scrubbed, with never-tiring energy and good-will. The raccoon worked very hard indeed: he said so, and nobody took the trouble to contradict him. He swept the kitchen occasionally, and did a good deal of graceful and genteel dusting with his long bushy tail, and tasted all the food that Bruin cooked, to see if it had the proper flavor. Besides these heavy duties, he caught rats, teased the cow, pulled the parrot's tail whenever he got a chance, and, as he expressed it, "tried to make things pleasant generally." The little squirrel had constituted himself a special attendant on "Madam," as the forest-friends all called the grandmother. He picked up her ball of yarn when it rolled off her lap, as it was constantly doing. He cracked nuts for her, brought her the spices and things when she made her famous gingerbread, and went to sleep in her ample pocket when he had nothing else to do. If you had taken off the covering and unrolled the ball, you would have found that it was a woodchuck, sound asleep. Poor Chucky had found it quite impossible to accept the new arrangement. He had always been in the habit of sleeping all through the winter; and while the other animals had succeeded, after a long time, in conquering their sleepiness (though it was still a very common thing to find Bruin asleep over the churn, and <DW53> had a way of creeping into Toto's bed at odd times during the day), the woodchuck had succumbed entirely after the first week, and had now been asleep for a couple of months. "Ah!" exclaimed the little squirrel, who had stationed himself on the top of Bruin's head, as a convenient and suitable place, "Ah! now this is what _I_ call comfort. Snowing fast outside, is isn't it, Bruin?" "Yes!" replied the bear. "That makes it all the more jolly inside!" said the squirrel. "What are we to do this evening? Is it a story evening, or dancing-school and games?" "We had dancing-school last night," said the bear. "I haven't got over it yet. I backed into the fire twice in 'forward and back, and cross over.' He lay still; waited and listened, listened and waited. After a little while there could be no doubt about it,--the four men were breathing heavily, slowly, regularly; and one of them rolled out a sonorous, a majestic snore, which resounded through the heavy perfumed air of the Temple, yet caused no movement among the other three. There could be no doubt about it,--the priests were asleep! Slowly, softly, the boy lifted his head; then he rose to his knees, and looked fearfully at the sleepers. He trembled, he turned white as the tunic which covered his dusky limbs; but standing erect, he gazed firmly at the Golden Dragon. From the floor rose a splendid altar of gold, studded thick with precious gems. Rubies, sapphires, and emeralds, set in mystic lines and figures, formed the characters which told the thirty-two names of the world-renowned dragon; and on the top of this glittering pedestal, fifteen feet in the air, stood the idol itself. It was, indeed, a marvellous thing to look upon. Ten feet long, composed entirely of thin scales of the purest gold, laid over and over each other, and each scale tipped with a diamond. Two magnificent rubies glowed in the eye-sockets, and the head was surmounted by a crown of emeralds worth any ordinary kingdom. But the tail! the tail was the wonder of wonders. Millions of delicate gold wires as fine as silk waved gracefully from the scaly tip a length of three feet, and each one was tipped with a diamond, a ruby, or an emerald of surpassing beauty and lustre.

Ten o'clock of a dark night. The outer gates of the royal palace were closed, though lights still shone in many of the windows. Outside the gate a sentinel was pacing up and down, armed with pike and broadsword. Every time he turned on his beat, he looked up and down the narrow street to see if anything or anybody were approaching. Suddenly, as he wheeled about, he saw before him a figure which seemed to have sprung all in a moment out of the blackness of the night. It was the figure of a boy, carrying a burden considerably larger than himself,--a dark and shapeless mass, which yet seemed not to be heavy in proportion to its size. "What is this?" cried the astonished sentinel. "Who art thou, and what monstrous burden is this thou carriest so lightly?" "Hist!" said the boy, speaking in an awestruck whisper, "speak not so loud, friend! This is the Celestial Footstool!" The sentinel recoiled, and stared in

The sentinel shook his head sadly, and resumed his walk; while Chop-Chin crept softly through the court-yard, keeping close to the wall, and feeling as he went along for a certain little door he knew of, which led by a staircase cut in the thickness of the wall to a certain unused closet, near the Celestial Bed-chamber. While all this was going on, the Emperor of China, the great and mighty Wah-Song, was going to bed. He had sipped his night-draught of hot wine mingled with honey and spices, sitting on the edge of the Celestial Bed, with the Celestial Nightcap of cloth-of-silver tied comfortably under his chin, and the Celestial Dressing-gown wrapped around him. He had scolded the Chief Pillow-thumper because the pillows were not fat enough, and because there were only ten of them instead of twelve. He had boxed the ears of the Tyer-of-the-Strings-of-the-Nightcap, and had thrown his golden goblet at the Principal Pourer, who brought him the wine. Once more the dreadful voice was heard:-- "Wah-Song! Wah-Song! Awake!" The Emperor sprang up in bed, and looked about him with eyes wild with terror. Ah! what was that?--that glittering form standing at the foot of his bed; that crowned head raised high as if in anger; those glaring red eyes fixed menacingly upon him! "Ah, horror! ah, destruction! the Golden Dragon is here!" With one long howl of terror and anguish, His Celestial Majesty Wah-Song rolled off the bed and under it, in one single motion, and lay there flat on his face, with his hands clasped over his head. Quaking in every limb, his teeth chattering, and a cold sweat pouring from him, he listened as the awful voice spoke again. "Wah-Song!" said the Golden Dragon, "thou hast summoned me, and I am here!" "Listen!" said the Dragon, sternly, "and venture not to speak save when I ask thee a question. Yesterday morning, in consequence of thine own caprice in going out unannounced, thy silly shoes and thy pusillanimous petticoat became wet. For this nothing, thou has condemned to death my faithful servant Ly-Chee, who has brought me fresh melons every Tuesday afternoon for thirty years. When others, less inhuman than thou, interceded for his life, thou madest reply, 'We swear, that unless the Golden Dragon himself come down from his altar and beg for this man's life, he shall die!'" The Emperor groaned, and clawed the carpet in his anguish. "Therefore, Wah-Song," continued the Dragon, "I AM HERE! I come not to beg, but to command. Dost thou hear me?" records.s: . Ten minutes later, the sentinel at the gate was amazed at the sight of the Chief Cabinet-maker's apprentice, reappearing suddenly before him, with his monstrous burden still in his arms. The boy's hair was dishevelled, and his face was very pale. In truth, it had been very hard work to get in and out of the hollow golden monster, and Chop-Chin was well-nigh exhausted by his efforts, and the great excitement which had nerved him to carry out his bold venture. "How now!" cried the sentinel. "What means this, boy?" "Alas!" said Chop-Chin, "alas! unhappy that I am! Was it my fault that the mended leg was a hair-breadth shorter than the others? Good soldier, I have been most grievously belabored, even with the Sacred Footstool itself, which, although it be a great honor, is nevertheless a painful one. And now must I take it back to my master, for it broke again the last time His Celestial Majesty brought it down on my head. Wherefore let me pass, good sentinel, for I can hardly stand for weariness." "Pass on, poor lad!" said the good-natured soldier.

"And yet--stay a moment! thinkest thou that aught would be amiss if I were to take just one peep at the Celestial Footstool? Often have I heard of its marvellous workmanship, and its tracery of pearl and ebony. Do but lift one corner of the mantle, good youth, and let me see at least a leg of the wonder." "At thy peril, touch it not!" cried the boy, in great alarm. "Knowest thou not that the penalty is four hundred lashes? Not a single glance have I ventured to cast at it, for they say its color changes if any profane eye rest upon its polished surface." "Pass on, then, in the name of the Dragon!" said the sentinel, opening the gate; and bidding him a hasty good-night, Chop-Chin hurried away into the darkness. "Speak!" said the chief priest in great agitation, "what is your errand?" "O Priest!" said the black guards, trembling with excitement, "we heard a great knocking at the gate." "Yes, yes!" cried the priest, "I know it. What more?" "O Priest!" said the guards, "we were affrighted, so great was the noise; so we opened the gate but a little way, and peeped through; and we saw--we

"Speak, sons of pigs!" shrieked the priest, "_what_ did you see?" "We saw the Golden Dragon!" said the soldiers, in a fearful whisper. "He is sitting up--on his hind-legs--with his mouth open! and he knocked--he knocked--" But the priests of the Saki-Pan waited to hear no more. In the midst of the troop rode Ly-Chee, on a splendid black horse. He was dressed in a robe of crimson satin embroidered with gold, and round his neck hung strings of jewels most glorious to see. "Tell us about your father, Miss Mary!" exclaimed the squirrel. "Fine old bird he must have been, eh?" "He was, indeed!" replied the parrot, with some emotion. "He was a noble bird. His beak, which I am said to have inherited, was the envy of every parrot in Central Africa. He could whistle in nine languages, and his tail--but as the famous poet Gabblio has sweetly sung,-- "'All languages and tongues must fail, In speaking of Polacko's tail.' "Polacko was my father's name," she explained. "He was universally respected. Ah, me!" "But how came he to go to China?" asked Toto. "He was captured, my dear, and taken there when very young. He lived there for twenty years, with one of the chief mandarins of the empire. After exchanging mutual "good-nights," the other members of the family sought their respective sleeping-places. The birds flew to their perches, and each, tucking her head and one leg away in some mysterious manner, became suddenly a very queer looking creature indeed. "<DW53>," said Toto, "come and sleep on my bed, won't you? My feet were cold, last night, and you do make such a delightful foot-warmer." "Humph!" said the raccoon, doubtfully. "I don't know, Toto. It won't be as warm for _me_ as my basket, though no doubt it would be nice for you." "I'll put the big blue dressing-gown over you," said Toto. "You know you like that, because you can put your nose in the pocket, and keep it warm." "All right," cried the raccoon. "Come along, then!" and off they went.

It is always a good thing for any one who has eyes in his head, but it is especially good when you see all that <DW53> and Toto saw; when you know, from every tiny track or footmark, what little creatures have been running or hopping about; when many of these little creatures are your friends, and all of them at least acquaintances. How fresh and crisp the air was! how soft and powdery and generally delightful the snow! What a pleasant world it was, on the whole! "Let me see!" said the raccoon, stopping and looking about him. "It is just about here that Chucky's aunt lives. Yes, I remember, now. You see that oak-stump yonder, with the moss on it? Well, her burrow is just under that.
